fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Professor Andrew Seidl plays a global leadership role as Senior Technical Advisor to the Biodiversity Finance Initiative. Through this work, he supports countries around the world in designing and implementing innovative finance solutions to close critical funding gaps for biodiversity conservation.

The Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN), led by the United Nations Development Programme, helps governments assess their biodiversity finance needs, reform policies, and mobilize new public and private investment to protect ecosystems and achieve global conservation targets. Seidl contributes technical expertise in economic valuation, policy design, and finance strategies, helping translate complex environmental challenges into actionable, country-level investment plans.

His work spans global research, capacity building, and on-the-ground advising, advancing a shift in how nations value nature and integrate biodiversity into economic decision-making. Through BIOFIN, these efforts have contributed to billions of dollars in financing for nature and support a growing international movement to align financial systems with sustainability and conservation goals.

Brief Summary.value: Professor Seidl advises BIOFIN, helping countries design finance solutions for biodiversity conservation, reform policies, and mobilize investment, advancing global efforts to integrate nature into economic decision-making.

The Colorado GROW Youth Institute is a statewide program that empowers high school students to explore and address pressing food security challenges locally and globally. Launched in 2024 in partnership with the World Food Prize Foundation, the program engages students in researching a global challenge, producing a paper, and presenting their ideas in roundtable discussions with peers and professionals at the annual event hosted at the CSU Spur campus.

Participants also engage in interactive, hands-on learning and explore academic and career pathways at the intersection of agriculture, sustainability, and food security. Outstanding student presenters are selected to represent Colorado as delegates at the World Food Prize Foundation’s Global Youth Institute. All participants are considered for scholarships to CSU's College of Agricultural Sciences and may apply for additional opportunities provided by the World Food Prize Foundation.

Beyond the annual event, the program fosters continued leadership development for alumni and provides educators with resources and support to integrate the Global Challenge curriculum into their classrooms.

Brief Summary.value: The Colorado GROW Youth Institute empowers high school students to address food security challenges through research, presentations, hands-on learning, and leadership development, with opportunities for scholarships and global engagement.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
This research collaboration between Heifer International, Professor Nick Magnan, and other academic collaborators examines how hybrid distance learning can expand access to vocational training for rural women in Nepal. The project focuses on training women to become community animal health workers (CAHWs)—a critical but hard‑to‑access profession in remote areas where women face mobility constraints and heavy household responsibilities. Traditional CAHW certification requires 35 consecutive days away from home, a barrier that limits women’s participation.

To address this, the team partnered with Heifer International and the Government of Nepal to design a hybrid training model combining short in‑person modules with tablet‑based home learning. Women completed a five‑day orientation and a ten‑day practical livestock module, while the remainder of the curriculum—covering animal health, breeding, disease diagnostics, and bookkeeping—was delivered remotely.

A randomized evaluation led by Magnan and colleagues found that hybrid training increased completion rates from 30% to 51% without compromising knowledge, skills, or long‑term job performance. Their findings demonstrate that well‑designed distance learning can meaningfully reduce gendered barriers to professional training and expand economic opportunities for rural women in Nepal.

Brief Summary.value: A hybrid distance learning model increased rural Nepali women’s completion of animal health worker training, reducing gender barriers and expanding economic opportunities without compromising knowledge or job performance.

Students engage in experiential learning through field-based activities and required excursions that connect classroom concepts to real-world contexts across Florence and the surrounding countryside.

Beyond academics, participants experience daily life in Italy, gaining firsthand insight into local food systems, regional culture, and the role of place in economic development, while building a global perspective on agriculture, sustainability, and international markets.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
For the approximately three quarters of the world’s poor who live in rural areas of low-income countries, agriculture and livestock are key for household income and economic growth. Opportunities to sell livestock to meat producers for revenue offer a channel for households to turn illiquid assets into liquid ones, bolstering household income and enabling consumption smoothing. Livestock are therefore an important asset and caring for their health is an economic investment. And yet, households face constraints in caring for their livestock and selling them. Veterinary care for household animals in poor, rural areas is limited, constrained by a low supply of knowledgeable animal health workers. Rural households face challenges in coordinating and executing sales to meat producers, constrained by diffuse communication networks and information asymmetries between buyers and sellers.

In this study, Dr. Magnan used a randomized controlled trial to test the effect of the introduction of two novel digital technologies to livestock cooperatives in rural Nepal. The first tool, an app ecosystem called “Digital Collective Marketing” is aimed at reducing information frictions in the market for goats raised by farmers in rural cooperatives and sold to urban meat producers. The second tool, a mobile app called “Digital Mentoring and Continuing Education”, is aimed at improving the knowledge and skills of community animal health workers who care for the health of the goats of farmers in these cooperatives.

Brief Summary.value: This study tested two digital tools in rural Nepal to improve livestock sales and animal health by reducing market information gaps and enhancing training for community animal health workers.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
As wildfire activity increases globally, understanding how fire alters the carbon cycle has become increasingly important. Through the SPECTRA project, funded by the UK Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) and conducted in collaboration with researchers in France, the University of Stirling, and Gabon's National Parks Agency, Dr. Francesca Cotrufo has helped address a critical knowledge gap: how fire transforms plant biomass into pyrogenic carbon (PyC), or charcoal, and how that material influences long-term soil carbon storage and climate.

Working in Gabon's fire-managed grasslands, the team examined the effects of different fire regimes on soil carbon dynamics, measuring soil organic matter fractions, quantifying pyrogenic carbon stocks, and using radiocarbon dating to determine the age and persistence of fire-derived carbon in soils. The project has produced a unique dataset that is helping advance both empirical and modeling research on fire-derived carbon.

Building on field measurements and soil incubation experiments conducted in Gabon, Cotrufo's team is using the data to develop and validate MEMS-PyC, the first process-based model designed to explicitly represent the formation, persistence, and fate of pyrogenic carbon in soils. Led by collaborators at the University of Stirling and supported by students and modelers in the MEMS team, this work is improving scientific understanding of how charcoal contributes to long-term carbon storage, how fire affects future soil carbon transformations, and how changing fire regimes may influence climate-carbon feedbacks in fire-prone ecosystems around the world.

Brief Summary.value: The SPECTRA project studies how fire transforms plant biomass into charcoal, affecting soil carbon storage and climate, and develops models to predict fire’s impact on global carbon cycles.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Professor Todd Gaines serves as director of the International Weed Genomics Consortium (IWGC), a global collaboration that brings together researchers, industry partners, and agricultural professionals to advance the understanding of weed biology through genomics. Founded in 2021 with support from the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research (FFAR) and industry sponsors, the consortium addresses weed management as a worldwide agricultural challenge by developing genomic resources that are openly available to researchers across the globe. Under Gaines’ leadership, the IWGC provides scientific guidance for genome sequencing and annotation projects, facilitates international collaborations, and connects researchers to opportunities for training, publications, and shared research initiatives. The consortium has grown into a network of more than 500 scientists and stakeholders spanning over 50 countries.

In addition to leading the consortium’s scientific agenda, Gaines plays a key role in building the global weed science community through conferences, workshops, and training programs. The IWGC regularly hosts educational events that help researchers and students develop expertise in genomics tools and applications, while also creating opportunities to establish new international partnerships. Since its launch, the consortium has become a recognized leader in weed genomics, supporting the sequencing of dozens of economically important weed species and providing a platform where scientists can share data, resources, and best practices. Through this combination of leadership, training, and community-building, Gaines has helped position the IWGC as a central hub for advancing weed science worldwide.

Brief Summary.value: Professor Todd Gaines leads the International Weed Genomics Consortium, advancing global weed genomics research, training, and collaboration, supporting genome sequencing, and building a worldwide network of over 500 scientists.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Soil is one of our most valuable natural resources, and soil organic matter is the foundation of its productivity, resilience, and climate benefits. Yet managing soils without knowing how much organic carbon they contain is like trying to manage a bank account without knowing the balance. Recognizing this challenge, Dr. Francesca Cotrufo's collaboration with the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) and her long-time colleague Dr. Emanuele Lugato helped transform understanding of soil carbon across Europe through the EU's LUCAS Soil Survey, which collected approximately 20,000 harmonized soil samples across the continent to create the first consistent inventory of European soils.

Building on this unprecedented dataset, Cotrufo's team applied advanced soil organic matter fractionation methods to distinguish between different forms of carbon storage. Using detailed laboratory measurements, statistical analyses, and machine learning approaches, they scaled their findings from a subset of samples to produce continental-scale maps of soil carbon fractions across Europe's diverse ecosystems.

The research identified where carbon is stored most securely, where it is most vulnerable to climate change and land-use pressures, and where opportunities exist to increase soil carbon sequestration. These insights have provided a scientific basis for climate-smart land management and EU policy decisions by helping target regions at greatest risk of carbon loss and those with the highest potential for improvement. Cotrufo is excited about the analyses they are currently preforming in her Soil Innovation Laboratory, as the LUCAS sites have been resampled, creating a powerful opportunity to directly measure changes in soil carbon over time and assess how different ecosystems are responding to management and climate change.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Cotrufo’s team mapped soil carbon across Europe, identifying secure and vulnerable areas, guiding EU climate policy, and enabling direct measurement of soil carbon changes through resampling and advanced analysis.

The key differences between introduced species that become harmful invaders and those who do not is an ongoing research question. In this project, Hufbauer and colleagues from France, New Zealand, and Australia study whether species that adapt to human-altered environments in their native regions are more likely to thrive in similar environments when introduced elsewhere.

By combining field sampling, genetic analysis, and environmental data, the team examines how human activities such as land use change shape the traits that help species spread. Their findings show how these human-driven conditions can create predictable patterns that favor certain species becoming invasive.

This research helps scientists better understand and anticipate biological invasions, improving our ability to prevent and manage invasive species that can harm ecosystems, agriculture, and economies.

Brief Summary.value: Researchers study if species adapted to human-altered environments are more likely to become invasive elsewhere, using fieldwork and genetics to predict and manage harmful biological invasions.

Professors Mark Enns and Scott Speidel in the Department of Animal Sciences are collaborating with cattle farmers and scientists in Peru to improve animal longevity and ultimately meat and milk production in high-altitude herds through targeted genetic research. Early efforts to introduce North American genetics selected for high milk production led to an unexpected challenge: increased calf mortality with some farmers experiencing mortality rates of 70–80% due to pulmonary hypertension, a condition linked to low-oxygen environments at high elevations.

Working alongside veterinarian and professor Timothy Holt from Colorado State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Enns and Speidel are helping address this issue by training local veterinarians and industry professionals to identify and select cattle naturally adapted to high-altitude conditions. This approach enables farmers to build herds that are both more productive and better suited to their environment, improving animal health, reducing losses, and strengthening livelihoods in Andean communities.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Artificial intelligence is emerging as a powerful tool for discovering new herbicides. Dr. Franck Dayan has partnered with Agrematch, an Israel-based AI chemistry company, to test and validate the mode of action of chemical structures flagged by their algorithms. In one project, the team validated several novel herbicides as PPO inhibitors, a mechanism that kills weeds by blocking a crucial enzyme to cause a fatal buildup of toxic compounds. While this mode of action is already known, the AI successfully identified unconventional chemical structures that researchers would not normally expect to target the enzyme.

The collaboration also discovered a natural herbicide called rhein, which inhibits photosynthesis similarly to paraquat by disrupting the electron transport chain and destroying cell membranes. While paraquat is notoriously dangerous—a single teaspoon can be lethal and lacks an antidote, prompting global bans—rhein is remarkably safe and occurs naturally in common food sources. Beyond these scientific findings, the research provided foundational career experience for two graduate students who co-authored publications based on the results.

Brief Summary.value: AI-driven research with Agrematch identified novel herbicides and a safe, natural alternative to paraquat, while providing valuable research experience and publication opportunities for graduate students.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Through a USDA NIFA-funded partnership with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines, University Distinguished Professor Jan Leach's lab is exploring an overlooked question: how do disease-resistant rice plants affect not just harmful pathogens, but also the beneficial microbes that live in, on and around the plant. The issue is similar to what happens in humans when we take antibiotics. While antibiotics kill harmful bacteria, they can also disrupt the body’s healthy microbial community.

The Leach lab is asking whether breeding crops for disease resistance has a similar unintended effect. When plants are bred to resist disease, they activate defense responses that produce chemicals that help fight off pathogens—but those same chemicals may also reshape the plant’s microbiome. Until now, little attention has been paid to these broader impacts. To address this gap, the team is studying rice plants with different resistance genes and tracking how their microbial communities change over time. They are also examining how these changes affect plant health and performance in the long term.

This work has implications beyond plant disease. Rice paddies are one of the world's largest agricultural sources of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Methane is produced not by the rice plants themselves, but by specialized microbes living in the flooded soil and around rice roots. The composition of these microbial communities can influence how much methane is generated and released into the atmosphere. By understanding how disease-resistance traits alter plant-associated microbial communities, researchers may uncover new strategies to reduce methane emissions while maintaining strong disease resistance.

In collaboration with partners in Taiwan, the CSU-IRRI team is measuring how resistance-related changes in the rice microbiome affect methane production and emissions. Together, this research is opening a new way of thinking about crop improvement—one that considers not only the genetics of the plant, but also the microbial communities that support it, with important implications for both global food security and climate resilience.

Brief Summary.value: Leach lab studies how breeding rice for disease resistance impacts beneficial microbes and methane emissions, aiming to improve crop health, reduce greenhouse gases, and enhance food security and climate resilience.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Plant breeders have traditionally focused on single disease resistance genes, essentially acting as “generals” , that detect pathogens and signal downstream genes to mount a defense response. However, pathogens evolve over time to overcome these resistance genes, limiting the durability of this strategy. To address this challenge, University Distinguished Professor Jan Leach's lab is advancing a novel approach that shifts focus from the “generals” to the downstream “soldier” genes that execute defense responses. Rather than relying on pathogen recognition alone, this strategy enhances how effectively defense genes respond once triggered. By selecting for stronger gene promoters, the team aims to amplify and broaden activation of defense pathways, resulting in more robust and durable resistance. As Leach notes, “It actually works - we’ve shown we can select for better promoters of those genes, and it makes the plants more resistant.”

Support from the Foundation for Food and Agricultural Research has enabled an ongoing international collaboration with the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) in Colombia. This partnership includes Colorado State University, the Universidad de Los Andes (Colombia), and the French National Research Institute for Sustainable Development (IRD). The project has delivered both scientific and capacity-building outcomes. It has generated genome sequences of key rice varieties and demonstrated the ability to identify and target genomic regions associated with enhanced defense responses. It has also trained graduate students and research associates across partner institutions and CGIAR centers. A three-day workshop at CIAT introduced plant breeders from across Latin America to this new strategy. Importantly, the project has fostered new and ongoing interdisciplinary and international collaborations.

Brief Summary.value: Leach’s lab developed a novel plant breeding strategy targeting defense gene promoters for durable disease resistance, supported by international collaboration, genome sequencing, and capacity-building workshops for Latin American plant breeders.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Dr. Franck Dayan is a leading researcher advancing the understanding of herbicides and herbicide resistance. His work focuses on discovering how herbicides function at the biochemical and molecular levels, identifying new herbicide targets, and developing strategies to combat the growing problem of herbicide-resistant weeds. In a project sponsored by Bayer, Dayan and a graduate student, Hudson Takano, investigated the molecular effects of an herbicide called glufosinate, which causes plants to build up a toxic chemical, eventually kiling it. By combining glufosinate with another type of herbicide, PPO herbicide, they discovered a way to kill weeds with significantly less herbicides, only 1/2 of the glufosinate and 1/30 of the PPO herbicide for the same level of effectiveness. This research resulted in patents held internationally for the combination of the herbicides. Dayan's research supports the development of more effective and sustainable weed management practices, helping protect agricultural productivity while reducing the long-term impacts of herbicide resistance.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Quinoa is a traditional Andean crop with increasing global importance because of its nutritional value, drought tolerance, and potential role in climate-resilient agriculture. As quinoa production expands beyond its center of origin, however, growers are encountering new pest challenges that require locally adapted integrated pest management strategies. This project connects emerging quinoa pest issues in North America with the longer history of quinoa cultivation and pest management in Peru and the broader Andean region.

In collaboration with Prof. Luis Miguel Cruces at the Universidad Nacional Agraria La Molina in Lima, Peru, Dr. Szczepaniec's team is comparing quinoa pest management across Andean and North American production systems. This work has led to a collaborative manuscript, Quinoa pest management across continents: Lessons from Andean systems and emerging threats in North America, which examines how pest complexes differ between long-established Andean systems and newer quinoa production regions in the United States. The project highlights shared priorities, including improved monitoring, biological control, host plant resistance, and regionally appropriate IPM tools. 

This collaboration is also creating a foundation for future comparative research on whether quinoa varieties grown in Peru may express stronger resistance to emerging pests affecting quinoa production in the United States, including the stem-boring fly Amauromyza karli. More broadly, the project supports international scholarly exchange and helps build pest management strategies informed by both Andean experience and emerging North American production needs.

Brief Summary.value: This project compares quinoa pest management in Andean and North American systems, identifying shared priorities and fostering international collaboration to develop regionally adapted, climate-resilient integrated pest management strategies.

The North American Agricultural Advisory Network (NAAAN) is hosting a first of its kind tri-national meeting in Regina, Saskatchewan May 11-13, 2027. Extension and rural advisory services play an important and unique role in the agricultural systems of Canada, Mexico, and the United States. The 2022 NAAAN baseline report, Feeding North America through Agricultural Extension, established a shared understanding of how extension contributes to the agricultural development of the three countries.

Building on that foundation, the 2027 Regina Convening will explore the future of extension and rural advisory services across North America – Addressing Challenges to Thrive. The convening is grounded in the recognition that many of the region’s most pressing challenges are shared. Pathogens, natural disasters, and extreme weather events don’t stop at national borders. By sharing knowledge, innovations, and response strategies across the continent, we can help strengthen resilience and food security. 

The convening is designed to foster strategic awareness and collaboration in extension and rural advisory services among business leaders, policymakers, researchers, producers, and community organizations across emerging technologies, creative financing for agriculture, biodefense and disaster preparedness, and water management and soil health.

Brief Summary.value: NAAAN’s 2027 tri-national meeting in Regina will unite leaders to address shared agricultural challenges, foster collaboration, and explore innovations in extension, technology, financing, disaster preparedness, and resource management.

Myrtle rust is a plant disease caused by the fungus Austropuccinia psidii. It threatens forests, native ecosystems, and agricultural production around the world, affecting important plants such as eucalyptus, guava, and many other members of the myrtle family. In Australia, which is home to a remarkable diversity of myrtle species, the disease has caused severe ecological damage and contributed to the loss of some native plants. In Hawaiʻi, myrtle rust affects ʻōhiʻa (Metrosideros polymorpha), a culturally and ecologically important evergreen tree that is already under pressure from other diseases.

Over the past several decades, myrtle rust has spread rapidly and is now found on every continent except Antarctica. Research has shown that the fungus exists in several genetically distinct groups, some of which can infect a wide range of plant species and spread across large geographic areas. Climate-based modeling has also identified regions around the world that may be vulnerable to future invasions.

The Stewart Lab is developing rapid diagnostic tools that can identify different strains of the pathogen and support early detection and response efforts. They are also studying the fungus's genetics, biology, and evolutionary history to better understand how highly invasive strains emerge and adapt to new environments. By identifying factors that contribute to the pathogen's spread and locating regions at greatest risk, their work helps inform targeted disease management strategies and supports the protection of forests, biodiversity, and agricultural systems worldwide.

Brief Summary.value: The Stewart Lab develops rapid diagnostics and studies myrtle rust genetics to inform targeted management, aiming to protect forests, biodiversity, and agriculture from this globally invasive plant disease.

Title (Links).value: Development of DNA-based, diagnostic tools to detect and identify invasive forest pathogens in the field and ports of entry

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Airborne pathogens pose a constant threat to tree propagation facilities crucial for forest restoration and conservation. To better understand and predict these threats, the Stewart Tree Pathology Lab is collaborating with institutions across the U.S. (USDA Forest Service), Europe, and Asia to track aerobiome microbes and their dynamics in nurseries and arboreta across contrasting climate zones using the innovative Airborne Threats Monitoring System (ATMoS), designed by CSU CAS PhD student Almendra Astete-Farfan. The Airborne Threats Monitoring System (ATMoS) is a low-cost, low-volume air sampler that uses specialized filters to capture airborne microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes. Microorganisms on the filters are analyzed through tagged meta-barcoding to characterize the aerobiome, and evaluate how airborne microbial communities change over time and across environmental conditions.

Airborne pathogens can cross geographic boundaries, and their dynamics may vary with climate, plant communities, and management practices. Collaborating across North America, Europe, and Asia allows the lab to compare diverse propagation facilities and identify both common and region-specific factors influencing airborne pathogen communities. By identifying environmental and management factors associated with airborne pathogens, this tool improves disease surveillance and management in nurseries and propagation facilities, ultimately helping reduce pathogen spread and protect forests, restoration programs, and plant collections worldwide.

Brief Summary.value: The Stewart Tree Pathology Lab uses ATMoS to monitor airborne pathogens in nurseries worldwide, improving disease surveillance and management to protect forests and restoration programs across diverse climate zones.

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content: Dr. Lovreet Singh Shergill is the first author of a chapter in an international book on harvest weed seed control (HWSC), leading the conceptualization, organization, and synthesis of the chapter. The chapter provides a global synthesis of research, practical experience, and regional case studies examining how HWSC is being evaluated and implemented across diverse cropping systems and agricultural regions. The chapter examines the opportunities and constraints associated with HWSC across different regions and crops, highlighting where the approach is well suited, where adoption and evaluation are still emerging, and how local weed biology, harvest practices, and farming systems influence its effectiveness. It contributes to the broader objective of documenting the global development, adoption, and future potential of HWSC as a sustainable weed management strategy.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Shergill authored a global synthesis chapter on harvest weed seed control, analyzing research, case studies, and regional adoption to assess HWSC’s effectiveness and future potential in sustainable agriculture.

Title (Links).value: How Harvest Weed Seed Control Works - GROW

fields.Project/Activity Summary - Story Content:
Dr. Daniel Burcham's research is helping cities make better, science-based decisions about the trees they plant and manage. In collaboration with researchers from New Zealand and Singapore, Burcham analyzed one of the world's largest urban tree inventory datasets to better understand how tropical tree species grow over their lifetimes. Their study, published in Urban Forestry & Urban Greening, examined 126 tree species across Singapore and revealed a fundamental trade-off in tree growth strategies: some species grow rapidly when young but slow substantially as they mature, while others grow more slowly early in life but maintain growth over longer periods. These patterns align with the well-known "fast-slow" spectrum in plant ecology and provide a biologically meaningful framework for understanding urban tree performance.

The research moves beyond simple growth predictions by identifying the life-history characteristics underlying tree development. Using advanced statistical modeling, the team generated growth parameters that can help urban foresters anticipate how different species will provide ecosystem services such as shade, cooling, carbon storage, and aesthetic benefits over time, while also forecasting maintenance needs and management costs. The findings offer a practical tool for selecting tree species based not only on expected growth rates but also on long-term growth strategies, helping cities design more resilient and sustainable urban forests. By connecting ecological theory with urban forestry practice, Burcham's work demonstrates how large municipal datasets can improve decision-making for greener and more livable cities.

Brief Summary.value: Dr. Burcham’s research uses large urban tree datasets to reveal growth strategies, helping cities select tree species for long-term resilience, ecosystem services, and sustainable urban forest management.
